items.subject: mental-health
items.explanation:
Opioids (e.g., morphine, oxycodone) are a group of medications most commonly used for pain relief. Their effects can be addictive, causing a high potential for abuse. Overdose of these medications depresses the central nervous system. The symptoms that are most commonly associated with overdose include:

  • Coma

  • Pinpoint (constricted) pupils

  • Severe respiratory depression which can lead to respiratory arrest and death

Additional symptoms may include hypothermia, hypotension, and bradycardia [Choice 3]. Naloxone is given to reverse the effects of an opioid overdose.

Incorrect:

Confused, diaphoretic, blood pressure of 150/90mmHg

Amphetamines (e.g., cocaine, Adderall) are central nervous system stimulants. Overdose produces symptoms of confusion, tachycardia, and diaphoreses. Hallucinations, paranoia, cardiac arrhythmia, and seizures are also possible.

Agitated, pulse of 120 bpm, diarrhea

Serotonin syndrome causes agitation, irritability, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and gastrointestinal symptoms like abdominal pain and diarrhea. It occurs due to excessive serotonin activity in the central nervous system, which results from an overdose of serotonergic medications such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) (e.g., fluoxetine, sertraline).

Slurred speech, labile mood, uncoordinated movements

Benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam, diazepam) are central nervous system depressants. Overdose symptoms include slurred speech, labile mood, and uncoordinated movements (i.e., ataxia). Additional symptoms of overdose include lethargy and confusion. Oral benzodiazepine overdoses alone are rarely fatal. However, severe respiratory depression and death can occur if mixed with other CNS depressants (e.g., alcohol, opiates).

Key Takeaway:

Classic presentation in opioid overdose includes:

  • Coma

  • Pinpoint pupils

  • Bradypnea

  • Other symptoms include hypothermia, hypotension, and bradycardia.
items.lead: The nurse is caring for a client who is suspected of attempting a medication overdose.
items.stem: Which of the following findings would support a diagnosis of an opioid overdose?
options: Confused, diaphoretic, blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg
Appears agitated, pulse of 120 bpm, and reporting diarrhea
Pinpoint pupils, temperature is 94.8 F (34.9 C), respirations of 8 per minute
Slurred speech, labile mood, movements are uncoordinated with unsteady gait

items.subject: fundamentals
items.explanation:
Restraints can be physical (e.g., mittens) or chemical (e.g., sedatives) and are used to keep clients safe; however, the nurse should always try less restrictive measures first.

The client is at risk for falls and should be given diversional activities to distract the client from attempting to get out of bed (e.g., magazines, folding towels, games, art) [Choice 2]. In addition, the nurse should schedule routine ambulation to assist the client to the bathroom and reduce the client’s attempts to get up alone.

Incorrect:

Decrease stimulation by turning lights off

Turning the lights off increases the risk for falls and injury if the client attempts to get out of bed. Additionally, confused clients need a well-lit environment during the day and evening to help reduce confusion and agitation associated with sundowning, which is the deterioration of cognitive functioning in clients with dementia in the afternoon and evening hours.

Insert indwelling urinary catheter

Lines, tubes, and drains (e.g., urinary catheters) increase the risk for infection and can increase the risk for falls when the client attempts to ambulate on their own. The nurse should frequently assist the client to the restroom.

Administer diphenhydramine to help client sleep

Antihistamines, like diphenhydramine, have anticholinergic effects, causing dizziness, drowsiness, and blurred vision. This could increase the risk for falls and confusion.

Key Takeaway:

Restraint alternatives include:

  • Scheduling ambulation and diversional activities

  • Limiting use of lines, tubes, and drains (e.g., urinary catheter) when possible
items.lead: The nurse is caring for a confused older adult client who is a fall risk and keeps attempting to get out of bed to go to the bathroom.
items.stem: Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
options: Decrease stimulation by turning off lights.
Give the client some magazines for reading.
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to limit bathroom trips.
Administer diphenhydramine at night to help the client sleep.

items.subject: mental-health
items.explanation:
Panic attacks are characterized by short episodes (15-30 minutes) of intense anxiety that escalate quickly and cause fear and physiological distress. Panic attacks may be triggered by a specific event or occur spontaneously, as seen with panic disorder. During a panic attack, clients may lose the ability to think rationally, which poses a safety risk.

Primary nursing interventions include staying with the client to ensure safety and decreasing environmental stimuli to prevent further escalation of anxiety (e.g., turning off the radio, closing the curtains) [Choice 3]. Anti-anxiety medications (e.g., benzodiazepines) may be considered if nonpharmacological interventions are ineffective.

Incorrect

Bring client into milieu

Bringing the client into a busy environment, such as the milieu, is inappropriate as it exposes the client to increased environmental stimuli. Ensuring a quiet environment by reducing external stimuli is the priority.

Ensure client stays seated

Clients experiencing panic attacks may feel too agitated to stay seated. Engaging the client in physical activity, such as walking or pacing, is appropriate to help expend this nervous energy and tension.

Breathe quickly

Clients experiencing panic attacks often feel like they cannot breathe, and breathing in and out quickly can result in hyperventilation. Instead, the nurse should use a low voice and clear, simple statements to guide the client in taking slow, deep breaths.

Key Takeaway:

When caring for a client experiencing a panic attack

  • Stay with the client to ensure safety.

  • Decrease environmental stimuli.
items.lead: The nurse is caring for a client who is experiencing a panic attack.
items.stem: Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
options: Ensure the client stays seated.
Bring the client out into the milieu.
Turn off the radio and close the curtains.
Coach the client to practice deep, rapid breathing.

items.subject: management-of-care
items.explanation:
The nurse should prioritize clients experiencing complications or those that are unstable. However, if all clients are stable, the nurse should prioritize tasks that can place the client at risk for immediate complications. Delaying administration of medications that help maintain hemodynamic stability and adequate circulation can have immediate health implications.

The nurse should first administer an overdue antihypertensive medication (e.g., labetalol, lisinopril) [Choice 1]. Delaying administration could worsen hypertension and potentially cause life-threatening complications (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction).

Incorrect:

Comfort crying client

Addressing a client’s emotional needs who has received distressing news is important. However, the client’s emotional upset does not pose an immediate risk to the client’s physical well-being. Therefore, this would not be the first priority.

Assess client with burning during urination

A burning sensation during initial urination following catheter removal is an expected finding due to urethral irritation from the catheter. The nurse should assess the client for other symptoms of a urinary tract infection (UTI) (e.g., fever, chills); however, this task would not take priority over a client at risk for worsening hypertension.

Perform discharge teaching

Although discharge teaching should be performed as soon as possible, a client who is stable enough for discharge can safely wait. The nurse should utilize therapeutic communication to alleviate the client’s frustration.

Key Takeaway:

  • When caring for stable clients, tasks that can result in immediate health complications, such as delaying an antihypertensive medication, should be prioritized to prevent life-threatening complications.
items.lead: The nurse has been made aware of the following client situations.
items.stem: Which of the following nursing actions should receive the highest priority?
options: Administer labetalol that was due 1 hour ago to a client with hypertension.
Comfort a client who is crying and upset following a diagnosis of a terminal illness.
Assess the client who reports mild burning with initial urination following indwelling catheter removal.
Provide discharge education to a frustrated client who has been requesting discharge paperwork for 3 hours.

items.subject: child-health
items.explanation:
Identity versus role confusion is the developmental task in Erikson’s psychosocial development theory for clients 12-20 years old. In this stage, clients should be encouraged to develop a sense of identity and purpose. Interventions promoting independence, relationships with peers, and self-discovery support this development.

The nurse should encourage clients to discuss their condition and its impact on their life and identity in a support group. A support group of peers with the same condition provides an educational opportunity and a chance to connect with peers [Choice 3].

Incorrect:

Write list of goals; Praise client

These interventions support Erikson’s industry versus inferiority stage, in which school-aged children (6-12 years old) learn skills and seek recognition, achievement, and competency. A 16-year-old client should be setting their own goals and not as motivated by praise as the school-aged client. Instead, the nurse should prioritize interventions that promote social interaction and identity development for adolescent clients.

Provide educational materials

Providing educational materials helps clients learn about their illness and how to manage it. However, merely providing materials does not actively engage the client in developing a sense of identity. Asking a client about how diabetes affects their life and engaging in an active discussion about their identity related to their diagnosis promotes a sense of identity.

Key Takeaway:

  • The nurse can support clients ages 12-20 years in Erikson’s identity versus role confusion stage by promoting exploration of identity and independence and facilitating relationships with peers.
items.lead: The nurse is caring for a hospitalized 16-year-old client with type 1 diabetes.
items.stem: Which of the following nursing interventions is most appropriate to facilitate a sense of identity?
options: Write a list of goals for the client to accomplish each day.
Praise the client for successfully self-administering insulin.
Encourage client to join a teen diabetic support group meeting.
Provide educational materials about diabetes-specific meal planning.

items.subject: management-of-care
items.explanation:
A tracheostomy is an artificial airway created by an opening in the trachea. Thick, copious tracheostomy secretions can obstruct airflow within the airway and cause coughing, an early sign of respiratory distress [Choice 3]. The nurse should immediately provide interventions to ensure a patent airway and prevent further respiratory distress (e.g., humidification, suctioning).

Incorrect:

Client with tonsillectomy and pain with swallowing

A tonsillectomy is surgical removal of the tonsils. Pain with swallowing is an expected finding immediately following a tonsillectomy. While the nurse should address the client’s pain, the client experiencing respiratory distress should be the first priority.

Client with Kawasaki disease and fever of 102.5°F (39.2°C)

Kawasaki disease (KD) is an acute, self-resolving vasculitis. The acute febrile stage of KD presents with high fevers. The nurse should continue to monitor the client’s vital signs and provide antipyretics and comfort measures, but immediate action is not required.

Asthma client with prescribed budesonide

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disorder. Inhaled corticosteroids (e.g., budesonide, beclomethasone) reduce airway inflammation. Administering scheduled medications is important but does not take priority over clients with potential airway complications.

Key Takeaway:

  • A client with copious airway secretions and coughing requires immediate intervention to prevent further respiratory distress.

  • Fever is an expected finding in the acute febrile stage of Kawasaki disease.

  • Pain with swallowing is common following a tonsillectomy.
items.lead: The nurse has received a change-of-shift report on the following pediatric clients.
items.stem: It would be a priority for the nurse to follow up with the
options: 7-year-old client recovering from a tonsillectomy who reports pain with swallowing
4-year-old client diagnosed with Kawasaki disease with a fever of 102.5°F (39.2°C)
6-year-old client with a tracheostomy who is coughing and has copious thick secretions
17-year-old client diagnosed with persistent asthma who had scheduled budesonide due 1 hour ago

items.subject: pharmacology
items.explanation:
Inhaled corticosteroids (e.g., beclomethasone, budesonide) control asthma by reducing airway inflammation. They are the treatment of choice for preventing asthma exacerbation in clients with mild persistent asthma.

Corrected teaching:

  • An inhaled corticosteroid should be taken daily to control asthma, regardless of whether symptoms are present [Choice 4]. Short-acting bronchodilators (e.g., albuterol), not inhaled corticosteroids, are indicated for immediate relief of symptoms and are taken as needed.

Statements that demonstrate understanding:

  • “I should rinse my mouth after I use my inhaler” [Choice 1].
    Inhaled corticosteroids increase the client’s risk for developing oral candidiasis, commonly referred to as thrush. Therefore, it is important to gargle and rinse out the mouth with water after use.

  • “This medication helps reduce the inflammation in my lungs” [Choice 2].
    Inhaled corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation and reactivity to triggers.

  • “After inhaling the medication, I should hold my breath for 10 seconds” [Choice 3].
    To administer the medication effectively, the client should hold their breath for at least 10 seconds after inhalation to allow the aerosol medication to reach deeply into the lungs.

Key Takeaway:

  • Inhaled corticosteroids, known as controller medications, must be taken daily to help reduce airway inflammation and prevent asthma exacerbations.

  • To use an inhaled corticosteroid, inhale, hold the breath for 10 seconds, exhale, then rinse the mouth to prevent candidiasis.
items.lead: The nurse is teaching a client who is newly prescribed inhaled beclomethasone.
items.stem: Which of the following statements by the client would require follow-up?
options: “I should rinse my mouth after I use my inhaler.”
“This medication helps reduce the inflammation in my lungs.”
“After inhaling the medication, I should hold my breath for 10 seconds.”
“I only need to use this inhaler when I don’t feel well and before I exercise.”

items.subject: management-of-care
items.explanation:
Advance directives are documents that outline a client's medical treatment decisions. These directives typically include a client’s code status decision. If a client wants to modify advance directives, the nurse should immediately notify the health care provider [Choice 2].

The health care provider is responsible for writing a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order. A DNR order is a health care provider’s directive stating a client's choice to decline CPR during cardiac or respiratory arrest. It does not exclude other treatments such as medications or nutrition.

Incorrect:

Update client’s record

Although advance directive documents should be placed in a client’s health record, changing the client to DNR status would not be appropriate without a health care provider’s DNR order.

Contact power of attorney (POA)

Although the POA may be contacted about the situation if the client wishes, the POA does not make decisions for the client who is able to verbalize a decision regarding care. POAs only make decisions for clients when the client is unable to do so.

Explain advance directives are permanent

Advance directives are not permanent and can be updated at any time. Additionally, the nurse should encourage client autonomy by allowing the client to make a decision. The client should not be persuaded to wait to document important decisions.

Key Takeaway:

  • Advance directives document a client’s treatment decisions.

  • The provider should be immediately notified of any changes to advance directives.

  • A do not resuscitate (DNR) status requires a provider order.
items.lead: The nurse is caring for an alert and oriented 32-year-old client with terminal cancer who states, “If something happens to me, don’t resuscitate me. Just let me go.”
items.stem: Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
options: Update the client’s health record to ensure the client’s decision is honored.
Contact the health care provider to notify them of the client’s updated decision.
Contact the client’s power of attorney to discuss updating the client’s resuscitation status.
Explain to the client that advance directives are permanent and to wait to make a decision.

items.subject: fundamentals
items.explanation:
An ostomy is a surgically created opening from the gastrointestinal tract onto the abdomen. A colostomy opens into the colon and occurs at various sites depending on the surgical reason (e.g., colorectal cancer, bowel perforation, diverticulosis).

The stoma is composed of intestinal tissue and is visible on the abdomen. Healthy stomas are shiny, red, and slightly edematous at first. A stoma that appears gray, dark red, bluish, or purplish indicates ischemia and should be reported to the health care provider immediately [Choice 2].

Incorrect:

Shiny, red, and edematous

A healthy stoma appears pink or beefy red, and moist, indicating optimal perfusion. Edema occurs from surgical manipulation and will subside in a few weeks, causing the stoma to be flush with the skin.

Slight serosanguineous drainage

Slight serosanguineous drainage from the stoma, especially when touched, is a normal finding due to the high vascularity of the area.

Protrusion 2 centimeters

New ostomies can protrude from the abdominal wall 1-2 centimeters because of edema from surgical manipulation. The ostomy will shrink in a few weeks and settle closer to the abdominal surface.

Key Takeaway:

  • Ostomies should be shiny, edematous, and pink or beefy red.

  • Ostomies that are gray, dark red, bluish, or purplish indicate ischemia.

  • New ostomies can have some serosanguineous drainage and edema in the first few weeks, causing stoma protrusion 1-2 cm.
items.lead: The nurse is assessing a client who had a colostomy 24 hours ago.
items.stem: Which of the following stoma findings would require immediate follow-up?
options: Shiny, red, and edematous
1-cm dark reddish-purple area
Slight serosanguineous drainage
Protrusion of 2 centimeters from abdominal wall

items.subject: adult-health
items.explanation:
When a client develops stroke-like symptoms, such as weakness and slurred speech, the nurse should first determine the presence or absence of lateralizing signs to help discern between a stroke or other systemic causes of stroke-like symptoms (e.g., delirium, hypoglycemia). Lateralizing signs, such as unilateral facial droop or arm weakness, are indicators of a neurological deficit on one side of the body, typically indicating a potential stroke instead of another systemic issue.

Performing a focused neurologic assessment, like asking the client to show their teeth, raise both arms, or speak a simple sentence, can provide immediate feedback on whether there is facial drooping or other lateralizing signs of a stroke [Choice 3]. This is a priority assessment to determine whether it is appropriate to activate the emergency stroke response team.

Incorrect:

Auscultate heart sounds

While it is always important to monitor heart sounds, especially after cardiac surgery, the client is experiencing neurological changes, not cardiovascular changes.

Notify primary health care provider (HCP)

While it may be necessary to notify the HCP, the nurse should first gather more information about the client's condition in order to give a complete telephone report.

Ask unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) to describe findings
It is outside the UAP scope of practice to assess and interpret client assessment data. Additionally, the UAP does not have the clinical judgement to determine the possible cause or severity of the client’s findings. Asking the UAP to further describe the abnormal findings would be inappropriate delegation and delay care.

Key Takeaway:

  • When a client develops stroke-like symptoms, the nurse should perform a focused neurological assessment to quickly assess for lateralizing signs of stroke (e.g., facial droop).

  • If lateralizing signs are present, the nurse should activate the stroke response team.
items.lead: The nurse and unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) are caring for a client who underwent a cardiac bypass graft yesterday. The UAP reports that the client has become "weak” and has developed slurred speech.
items.stem: Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
options: Auscultate the client’s heart sounds.
Notify the primary health care provider.
Perform a focused neurologic assessment.
Ask the UAP to describe the findings in more detail.

items.subject: child-health
items.explanation:
Adequate nutrition and healthy eating habits for pediatric clients ensure proper growth and development and promote a lifetime of good dietary decisions. Teaching centers around choosing balanced and appropriate meals and supporting a healthy relationship with food.

Teaching was effective if the caregiver demonstrates understanding of the following teaching:

  • Picky eating is common in young children as they learn to control their environment and develop independent thinking skills. Understanding a child’s preferences and routines allows parents to plan a balanced nutritional diet around a full week. It is important to offer a variety of nutritious foods throughout the week for optimal nutrition during this stage instead of trying to achieve the same variety within a single day [Choice 4].

Corrected teaching:

  • Food should not be used as a reward, as this encourages overeating for nonnutritive reasons [Choice 1].

  • “Clearing the plate” increases the likelihood of overeating and related health complications (e.g., childhood obesity). Providing smaller portions promotes healthy eating habits [Choice 2]. Children can have a second serving if they are still hungry.

  • Small, whole, round foods such as grapes, nuts, and circular pieces of hot dogs are choking hazards for infants and toddlers [Choice 3]. Soft foods may be cut into smaller pieces to decrease choking risk.

Key Takeaway:

  • To prevent overeating, do not force children to finish their meals or use food as reward.

  • Whole round foods (e.g., grapes, nuts) are choking hazards for young children.

  • Picky eating is a normal finding in young children.
items.lead: The pediatric nurse is providing education to caregivers regarding nutrition and eating habits in children.
items.stem: Which of the following caregiver statements shows understanding?
options: “I give my child ice cream when he gets a good grade in school.”
“My child must eat his entire plate of food before leaving the table.”
“A handful of grapes are an appropriate snack for my 11-month-old child.”
“It is okay if all my toddler eats is chicken nuggets and apples 2 days in a row.”

items.subject: adult-health
items.explanation:
Thrombocytopenia occurs when the circulating platelet count falls below 150 x 103/µL (150 x 109/L). Thrombocytopenia increases the risk of bleeding. Therefore, nursing care focuses on injury prevention and implementation of bleeding precautions, including:

  • Avoiding venipunctures and intramuscular (IM) injections. Alternative routes of administration, such as oral, should be used if available [Choice 4]. If an injection is necessary, the smallest appropriate needle should be used to minimize bleeding.

  • Monitoring for signs of bleeding (e.g., bruising, petechiae)

  • Reducing risk for physical trauma (e.g., fall prevention); applying ice if trauma occurs

Incorrect:

Aspirin

Medications that inhibit clotting (e.g., aspirin) should be avoided as they further increase bleeding risk. Non-aspirin-containing medications, like acetaminophen, should be considered instead.

Neutropenic precautions

Neutropenic precautions protect clients with neutropenia (i.e., low neutrophil count) from infection. Neutropenia and thrombocytopenia can present together in clients with bone marrow suppression; however, neutropenic precautions are unnecessary for thrombocytopenia alone.

Enema

Administering enemas or suppositories and taking rectal temperatures should be avoided as this can damage the rectal mucosa and result in bleeding. Instead, stool softeners (e.g., docusate) should be used to relieve constipation and prevent straining during bowel movements, which can increase intracranial pressure.

Key Takeaway:

Nursing care for thrombocytopenia includes:

  • Using stool softenings instead of enemas or suppositories

  • Avoiding medications that inhibit clotting (e.g., aspirin)

  • Avoiding venipunctures and intramuscular injections when possible
items.lead: The nurse is planning care for a client who has thrombocytopenia.
items.stem: Which of the following interventions should the nurse include in the client’s plan of care?
options: Administer aspirin as needed for pain.
Place the client on neutropenic precautions.
Administer an enema if needed for constipation.
Request an alternative route for intramuscular injections.

items.subject: fundamentals
items.explanation:
Nonrebreather masks deliver oxygen therapy for clients experiencing severe hypoxemia and requiring high oxygen concentrations (e.g., carbon monoxide poisoning, smoke inhalation). Nonrebreather masks require a 10-15 L/min flow rate to inflate the oxygen reservoir bag [Choice 1]. If the flow rate is insufficient, the client cannot inhale enough oxygen and is at risk for suffocation.

Incorrect:

Ensures reservoir bag fully inflates during exhalation

On exhalation, the oxygen reservoir bag should not inflate; instead, CO2 should escape from the mask. Meanwhile, oxygen should be retained within the partially inflated reservoir bag at all times. If the oxygen reservoir bag inflates during exhalation, it indicates a leak in the one-way valve between mask and bag. A valve leak allows exhaled CO2 into the oxygen reservoir bag, which the client would then rebreathe during the next breath.

Apply petroleum jelly

Petroleum jelly provides moisture and a barrier to prevent dry skin but could block oxygen flow and may create a fire hazard near an oxygen source. The nurse should apply sterile saline to moisten nasal cavities.

Ensures one-way valves remain closed during exhalation

The mask has external one-way valves that close with inhalation so that oxygen is inhaled from the bag and opened with exhalation to allow CO2 to escape from the mask.

Key Takeaway:

Non-rebreather masks:

  • Have bags that should remain partially inflated

  • Have valves that open on exhalation and close with inhalation

  • Require a 10-15 L/minute oxygen flow rate
items.lead: The nurse is preparing to administer oxygen via a non-rebreather mask for a client with hypoxemia.
items.stem: Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
options: Set the oxygen rate to 15 liters per minute.
Ensure the bag fully inflates during exhalation.
Apply petroleum jelly to the nares to prevent drying.
Ensure one-way valves on the facemask remain closed during exhalation.

items.subject: maternal-and-newborn-health
items.explanation:
This client is exhibiting manifestations of an obstetric emergency. Abdominal pain, signs of hypovolemia (e.g., heavy vaginal bleeding, maternal pulse [138], respiratory rate [24]), and signs of fetal distress (e.g., fetal heart rate [FHR] of 90) require immediate assessment [Choices 1, 2, 4, 6, and 7].

Current anticoagulant (i.e., enoxaparin) and antiplatelet use (i.e., aspirin) must also be immediately considered as this will increase the bleeding risk and influence treatment (e.g., need for protamine sulfate) [Choice 5].

Incorrect:

Facial laceration

The client may require stitches and possible antibiotics to prevent infection. Treating superficial lacerations (e.g., injury above deep veins) does not take priority over manifestations of an obstetric emergency.

History of cesarean section 15 months ago

Short intervals between pregnancies (<18 months), in addition to a previous uterine incision, increase the client’s risk for pregnancy complications (e.g., uterine rupture, placenta previa). Although these findings are important to consider, there is no indicated intervention for these risks, and they do not take priority over signs of an obstetric emergency.

Key Takeaway:

Signs of a possible obstetric emergency include:

  • Heavy vaginal bleeding

  • Severe abdominal pain

  • Fetal distress (FHR <110)

  • Tachycardia and tachypnea, which indicate hypovolemia
items.stem: Select the top 6 findings that would require immediate follow-up.
options: Fetal heart rate
Respiratory rate
Facial laceration
Maternal heart rate
Home medications
Lower abdominal pain
Heavy vaginal bleeding
History of cesarean section 15 months ago

items.subject: maternal-and-newborn-health
items.explanation:
Blunt abdominal trauma (e.g., fall) can injure vital organs, including the placenta and uterus. When fetal blood supply is interrupted (e.g., hypovolemia, placental injury), the fetus is deprived of oxygen and nutrients, resulting in fetal hypoxia and signs of distress (e.g., nonreassuring heart tones [prolonged or late decelerations, fetal bradycardia]).

This client is experiencing heavy vaginal bleeding (i.e., hemorrhaging) after blunt abdominal trauma from a fall. Therefore, the nurse recognizes that a decreased fetal heart rate is likely related to fetal hypoxia caused by hemorrhaging.

Incorrect:

Cervical os obstruction, Placenta previa

In placenta previa, the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment, completely or partially over the cervical os (opening). As this segment thins (i.e., effaces) and the cervix dilates, placental blood vessels are disrupted, resulting in painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding. This client is experiencing painful bleeding, indicating that placenta previa is unlikely.

Maternal tachycardia, Pulmonary embolism

The client’s history of pulmonary embolism (PE), tachycardia (HR 138), and tachypnea (RR 24) can indicate a PE. Maternal respiratory distress negatively affects oxygenation through the placenta to the fetus and can cause fetal hypoxia. However, she is not experiencing any other PE symptoms (e.g., chest pain, shortness of breath), and her pulse oximeter reading is normal (98%). In addition, she is taking enoxaparin prophylactically, making a PE unlikely.

Key Takeaway:

  • When the fetal blood supply is interrupted (e.g., trauma, hemorrhage), fetal hypoxia and subsequent distress (e.g., prolonged decelerations) can occur.
items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of optiions.
items.template: The nurse recognizes that a decreased fetal heart rate is likely related to {0} caused by {1}.

options: fetal hypoxia
cervical os obstruction
maternal tachycardia
hemorrhaging
placenta previa
pulmonary embolism

items.subject: maternal-and-newborn-health
items.explanation:
Uterine rupture happens when the uterine layers tear (endometrium, myometrium, perimetrium) and is often caused by abdominal trauma. This tear allows uterine and fetal components to enter the peritoneal cavity, potentially allowing palpation of fetal parts through the abdomen.

Uterine muscle tissue disruption results in poor uterine tone marked by weakened contractions and significant blood loss. This substantial bleeding can deprive the fetus of adequate oxygenation and nutrients, causing fetal distress.

Uterine scar tissue formed after prior cesarean sections is weaker than the surrounding uterine muscle. This makes areas with scar tissue more susceptible to rupture. Additionally, the risk of rupture increases when pregnancies occur within short intervals (<18 months) due to insufficient time for proper uterine healing.

Therefore, this client is most likely experiencing a uterine rupture.

Incorrect:

Placental abruption

Placental abruption occurs when the placenta detaches prematurely from the uterus, causing abdominal pain, dark red vaginal bleeding, and a rigid abdomen (i.e., hypertonicity). This client has poor uterine tone (i.e., hypotonicity) and palpable fetal parts on assessment, indicating uterine rupture, not an abruption.

Intrauterine fetal demise (IUFD)

An IUFD is fetal death occurring >20 weeks gestation. Although uterine rupture can lead to an IUFD, the FHR is 90 beats per minute, indicating that an IUFD has not occurred.

Key Takeaway:

  • A client with painful, bright-red bleeding; abdominal pain; fetal distress; palpable fetal parts; and poor uterine tone is likely experiencing uterine rupture.
items.stem:
The nurse reviews the Diagnostic Results and Nurses’ Notes from 1315.

Complete the following sentence by choosing from the list of options.
items.template: This client is most likely experiencing {0}.

items.subject: maternal-and-newborn-health
items.explanation:
Uterine rupture requires emergent cesarean section and circulatory volume replacement.

Indicated interventions include:

  • Administering IV fluids for circulatory volume replacement and maintenance; the client will have continued blood loss (e.g., surgery, postpartum) [Choice 1].

  • Notifying the anesthesiologist [Choice 2]. The anesthesiologist should be notified to prepare the client for emergent cesarean delivery (e.g., general anesthesia).

  • Obtaining blood for type and screen [Choice 3]. The nurse should anticipate a blood transfusion to replace the excessive blood loss.

  • Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter to empty the bladder during surgery and prevent bladder injury due to its proximity to the uterus [Choice 4].

  • Positioning supine with a wedge under the right hip [Choice 7]. The client should be positioned supine for emergency cesarean surgery. A hip wedge prevents the gravid uterus from compressing the vena cava, which can cause hypotension and reduced fetal circulation.

Interventions not indicated include:

  • Administering betamethasone injection [Choice 5]. Betamethasone is a corticosteroid administered as a two-part injection 24 hours apart to promote fetal lung development when preterm birth is a risk. Emergent delivery does not allow time for betamethasone.

  • Assessing cervical dilation and fetal station [Choice 6]. Cervical dilation and fetal station are unnecessary assessments and only useful in vaginal delivery.

Key Takeaway:

Interventions for uterine rupture include:

  • Cesarean delivery

  • IV fluid

  • Blood for type and screen

  • Indwelling urinary catheter

For each potential nursing intervention, click to specify whether the intervention is indicated or not indicated for the care of the client.

items.subject: maternal-and-newborn-health
items.explanation:
The client requires pain management and interventions to promote hemodynamic stability.

The client’s pain rating of 7/10 indicates uncontrolled pain; the nurse should administer IV hydromorphone [Choice 2].

The client continues to experience manifestations of hypovolemia that started before surgery (e.g., tachypnea, tachycardia, pallor, anxiety). After losing an additional 1,200 mL of blood during surgery, it is essential to administer packed red blood cells to replace fluid volume deficits and prevent shock [Choice 3].

Incorrect:

Reassess bowel sounds

General anesthesia can decrease bowel motility, causing hypoactive or absent bowel sounds. The nurse should continue to assess bowel sounds, but hypoactive bowel sounds are not prioritized before issues of circulation and pain.

Encourage incentive spirometer use

Incentive spirometry encourages deep breathing to clear fluid and anesthesia from the client’s lungs. However, pain and blood volume replacement should be addressed first to ensure hemodynamic stability.

Assist client to NICU to promote skin-to-skin contact

Promoting emotional bonding with the baby is important for the client’s well-being and milk supply. However, the client should be on bed rest until she is hemodynamically stable and her pain is under control.

Key Takeaway

  • The nurse should ensure that the client is hemodynamically stable (e.g., administering blood products) and pain is controlled before addressing less urgent concerns (e.g., skin-to-skin contact, incentive spirometry).
items.lead: The nurse reviews the Nurses’ Notes and Laboratory Results from 1600.
items.stem: Select the top 2 interventions that the nurse should perform first.
options: Reassess the client’s bowel sounds.
Administer 0.5 mg IV hydromorphone.
Administer 1 unit of packed red blood cells.
Encourage the use of the incentive spirometer.
Assist mother to the NICU to perform skin to skin.

items.subject: maternal-and-newborn-health
items.explanation:
This client requires postpartum and post-hysterectomy education.

The following indicates an understanding of teaching:

  • Routine pap smears for cervical cancer screening are recommended ≥21 years of age. A total hysterectomy removes the uterus and cervix; therefore, routine pap smears are no longer required [Choice 1].

  • Prophylactic enoxaparin is continued for 6 weeks postpartum due to the history of pulmonary embolism [Choice 2]. The client’s history, coupled with the hypercoagulable state of pregnancy and decreased mobility following cesarean section, increases the risk for blood clots.

Corrected teaching:

  • Clients experiencing menopause or oophorectomy (ovary removal) might require hormone replacement therapy to provide hormones no longer produced by the ovaries (e.g., estrogen, progesterone). A total hysterectomy only removes the cervix and uterus; therefore, hormone replacement is unnecessary since the ovaries remain intact [Choice 3].

  • Heavy vaginal bleeding can occur postpartum; however, changing the pad every hour is excessive and should be reported [Choice 4]. Vaginal peripads require replacement every couple of hours at most.

  • Postpartum baby blues are an expected finding characterized by periods of emotional lability resolving ≤10 days postpartum. Symptoms persisting >10 days indicate possible postpartum depression and require follow-up [Choice 5].

  • The client should avoid driving for 2 weeks post-surgery to allow incisional healing. Driving actions (e.g., turning head, moving legs) cause seat belt rubbing against the incision and could cause complications [Choice 6].

Key Takeaway:

Discharge instructions should include:

  • Avoid driving for 2 weeks.

  • Take anticoagulants as prescribed.

  • Monitor heavy bleeding and emotional state.

“If I feel depressed and anxious for the next month, that is caused by normal hormone fluctuations.”
“I’m sad that my baby needs to stay at the hospital, but I will be able to drive myself here anytime to visit him.”

items.subject: pharmacology
items.explanation:
Magnesium Sulfate Toxicity


Blood pressure decreased ↓


Urine output decreased ↓


Respiratory rate decreased ↓


Patellar reflex absent 🚫


Preeclampsia is characterized by maternal endothelial cell dysfunction, which causes vasoconstriction, hypertension, and increased vascular permeability, allowing fluid to leak from the vascular space into the tissue. This can cause cerebral edema, leading to central nervous system (CNS) hyperactivity and seizures (i.e., eclampsia).

Magnesium sulfate is administered to depress the CNS and prevent seizures. Additionally, it lowers blood pressure by relaxing vascular smooth muscle.

Magnesium sulfate infusions increase the risk for CNS and respiratory depression. Infusions should be stopped if the client experiences decreased urinary output, CNS depression (e.g., absent deep tendon reflexes), or respiratory depression (i.e., shallow or slow respirations [rate <12]) [Choice 1]. Calcium gluconate, an antidote for magnesium sulfate toxicity, may be needed.

Incorrect:

Continuous headache; Flashes of light

Cerebral edema can cause severe headaches and visual changes. While these signs may indicate worsening preeclampsia, these are expected findings in a preeclamptic client. Magnesium sulfate will improve these symptoms.

Urinary output 120 mL

Hypertension causes poor organ perfusion and can impair renal function. This increases the risk of magnesium toxicity, as the kidneys secrete magnesium. A urine output of 120 ml over 4 hours is adequate (i.e., minimum 30 mL/hr). Decreased urinary output would be concerning for significant renal impairment and decreased magnesium excretion that may contribute to toxicity.

Key Takeaway:

  • Magnesium sulfate infusions should be stopped if the client experiences decreased urinary output, CNS depression (e.g., absent deep tendon reflexes), or respiratory depression (i.e., shallow or slow respirations).
items.lead: The nurse is administering a magnesium sulfate infusion to a preeclamptic client and is preparing to administer a new bag.
items.stem: Which of the following findings would require immediate follow-up?
options: Respiratory rate of 10
Continuous headache
Blurred vision and flashes of light
Urinary output 120 mL over 4 hours

items.subject: mental-health
items.explanation:
During electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), an electrical current is passed through the brain, triggering a brief seizure. These seizures are thought to affect neurotransmitters (e.g., serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine) and alleviate symptoms of severe mood disorders when less invasive approaches have been unsuccessful (e.g., medications, therapy, lifestyle modifications).

Following ECT, clients experience a postictal phase, which refers to the recovery period immediately following seizure activity. During this phase, clients will likely experience confusion, disorientation, drowsiness, and temporary memory loss [Choice 3]. Therefore, the nurse should provide frequent reorientation in the recovery phase.

Incorrect:

“Eat meal before ECT”

Due to the use of generalized anesthesia and induction of seizure activity, clients must avoid oral intake for several hours before ECT to minimize the risk of vomiting and aspiration.

“Clients can drive”

Confusion and disorientation are common following ECT and can persist for several hours. Therefore, the client should be advised not to drive and to have someone stay with them for the remainder of the day.

“Bone fractures are common”

During ECT, general anesthesia and a skeletal muscle relaxant (i.e.,paralytic) are administered to prevent the strong muscle contractions that would otherwise occur from the seizure activity induced by ECT. Therefore, the risk of fractures is significantly reduced and does not commonly occur.

Key Takeaway:

ECT education includes:

  • No food or drink before the procedure

  • Confusion and disorientation are common

  • Clients should not drive following ECT

  • Muscle relaxant/paralytic is administered before ECT to reduce the risk of injury
items.lead: The nurse is planning a staff education program about electroconvulsive therapy (ECT).
items.stem: Which of the following information should the nurse include?
options: Educate clients to eat a well-balanced meal prior to arriving for this procedure.
Clients can drive themselves home from this procedure after a short recovery period.
Clients should frequently be reoriented following ECT because confusion is common.
Bone fractures are a common injury because of the seizure activity induced during ECT.

items.subject: management-of-care
items.explanation:
The nurse's role in the informed consent process is to serve as a witness that the client has voluntarily provided permission for treatment [Choice 2]. However, it's important to note that the nurse's role is primarily to witness the consent process, not to provide detailed education or obtain the consent itself.

Incorrect:

Provide consent after diazepam

A client should not provide consent following administration of a medication that alters their mental status (e.g., benzodiazepines, opioids), even if they appear oriented. The informed consent process should not be completed until the medication wears off.

If client refuses, emergency consent

Clients have the right to refuse treatment, and alternative options should be explored. Emergency consent is only appropriate in situations involving a life-threatening emergency when obtaining formal consent is not possible due to the client's critical condition (e.g., cardiac arrest, unconscious). Therefore, emergency consent would not be appropriate for a client refusing care.

Sign consent, education in surgery

Rushing the informed consent process and deferring education to the surgical unit is not appropriate. Informed consent requires that clients receive comprehensive information from the health care provider about treatment before signing, not from the nurse. Additionally, the client should be given an opportunity to ask treatment questions.

Key Takeaway:

  • The nurse's role in the informed consent process is to serve as a witness that the client is voluntarily providing consent.
items.lead: The nurse has attended a staff education program about informed consent.
items.stem: Which of the following statements by the nurse would indicate a correct understanding of the teaching?
options: “The client can provide consent after a recent dose of diazepam if the client is awake and alert.”
“As the nurse, I can witness that the client is providing consent for the procedure or treatment.”
“The next time a client refuses to sign an informed consent for a procedure, we can use emergency consent instead.”
“If the surgical team is in a hurry, I can get the consent signed, and the client can get more information in the surgical unit.”

items.subject: maternal-and-newborn-health
items.explanation:
Mastitis occurs when bacteria enter through cracked nipple tissue or grow from milk stasis (e.g., plugged duct), causing mammary gland inflammation. Symptoms include breast swelling; erythema; pain; a warm, palpable lump/mass; fatigue; and high-grade fever.

The nurse should administer antibiotics to treat the bacterial infection and provide education on applying heat/massaging before feeding/pumping to facilitate milk flow, reducing milk stasis.

The nurse should monitor for elevated white blood cell count (WBC) and drainage characteristics; purulent drainage would indicate worsening infection.

Incorrect:

Conditions:

  • Engorgement: Engorgement is breast swelling from excess milk production, causing tenderness but no fever.

  • Breast abscess: Breast abscesses are pus-filled masses resulting from unresolved mastitis. Purulent nipple drainage is absent, and symptoms just started, making abscess unlikely.

  • Inflammatory breast cancer (IBC): IBC, often mistaken for mastitis, is characterized by swelling, a lump/mass, skin dimpling, and nipple retraction but no fever.

Actions:

  • Drain lump: Surgical drainage treats breast abscesses, not mastitis.

  • Formula feed: Mastitis cannot pass through breast milk. Clients should continue to nurse/pump every 2-3 hours, promoting breast emptying.

  • Breast shields: Shields can prevent nipple damage, which allows bacterial entry, but will not improve infection.

Monitor:

  • Newborn jaundice; Newborn’s weight: Newborn weight loss and jaundice, indicating hyperbilirubinemia, can occur with inadequate intake, however, monitoring these will not evaluate treatment progress.

  • Nipple retraction: Nipple retraction occurs with IBC, not mastitis.

Key Takeaway:

  • Mastitis is a bacterial milk duct infection.

  • Treatment includes antibiotics and warm compresses.

  • Purulent nipple drainage and elevated WBC indicate worsening infection.
items.lead: The nurse reviews the History and Physical to prepare the client’s plan of care.
items.stem: Complete the diagram by dragging from the choices below to specify what condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take to address that condition, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client’s progress.

Prepare for the provider to drain the lump

items.subject: fundamentals
items.explanation:
Enemas instill fluid into the rectum to break up fecal matter and stretch the rectum, stimulating peristalsis and defecation. Enemas are used to relieve constipation or to prepare for procedures like a colonoscopy.

The nurse should begin administration by holding the bag of solution at the client’s hip level and slowly raising it higher. The higher the bag is held, the faster the solution will flow. Cramping may occur during enema administration as the enema distends the colon. If the client experiences discomfort, the nurse should pause and lower the bag before resuming to slow the rate [Choice 3].

Incorrect:

Change client’s position to prone

The client should be positioned left side-lying (Sims) with the right knee flexed and catheter tip pointed toward the umbilicus. Other positions could cause intestinal wall injury due to incorrect insertion angle.

Advance enema tube

The enema tube should be inserted 7-10 cm (3-4 inches) in adults; the depth varies for children. If there is resistance, have the client take deep breaths to relax the anal sphincter and continue.

Discontinue and notify provider

Cramping is an expected sensation that may occur during enema administration. The provider does not need to be notified.

Key Takeaway:

Enemas:

  • Can cause cramping, relieved by lowering the bag of solution

  • Are administered with the client in Sims position

  • Should be inserted 7-10 cm (3-4 in)
items.lead: The nurse is administering an enema to a client when the client reports painful cramping.
items.stem: Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
options: Change the client’s position to prone.
Advance the tube further into the colon.
Pause instillation and lower bag before resuming.
Discontinue instillation and notify health care provider.

items.subject: fundamentals
items.explanation:
Sleep hygiene refers to positive habits that promote consistent, good-quality sleep.

Teaching was effective if the client understands the following teaching points:

  • Adequate physical activity is important for maintaining good sleep quality; however, exercising within 3 hours of bedtime can interfere with the ability to fall asleep [Choice 1].

  • Eating a light snack before sleep prevents hunger, which can cause insomnia. Clients should avoid large meals before bed as digestion can last several hours, disrupting sleep [Choice 2].

  • The bed should only be used for sleep and sexual activity to promote restfulness. Clients should avoid reading and watching television in the bedroom as this associates wakefulness with being in bed [Choice 3].

Corrected teaching:

  • While diphenhydramine can cause drowsiness, it should not be used as a sleep medication. This could cause dependence and negative side effects (e.g., daytime drowsiness). Additionally, prescription sleeping medications should only be taken as needed in the lowest effective dose [Choice 4].

  • Clients should go to bed once they feel tired and avoid lying in bed awake. To maximize the likelihood of falling asleep quickly, clients can engage in relaxing activities outside of bed (e.g., reading, crossword puzzles) [Choice 5].

Key Takeaway:

Good sleep hygiene includes:

  • Engaging in daily physical exercise early in the day

  • Eating a light snack before bed

  • Avoiding reading in bed

  • Going to bed once tired

  • Using sleep medications only if necessary
items.lead: The nurse is educating a client with insomnia about the importance of sleep hygiene.
items.stem: Which client statements indicate that the teaching was effective? Select all that apply.
options: “I shouldn't lift weights late in the evening.”
“A light snack before bed is okay if I’m feeling hungry.”
“When I read at night, I should sit in my chair and not in my bed.”
“I can take diphenhydramine every night to ensure quality sleep.”
“I should go to bed by 9 p.m. and lay there to help make myself sleepy.”

items.subject: child-health
items.explanation:
The nurse should prioritize immediately stabilizing the neck in a neutral position until further assessment is completed [Choice 1]. Immobilizing the cervical spine prevents movements that can harm the spinal cord and cause permanent loss of sensory and motor function below the level of injury.

Rigid cervical collars prevent flexion, extension, and rotation of the spine with the goal of minimizing further injury to the spinal cord. Additional interventions can be completed once the cervical spine is immobilized.

Incorrect:

Obtain thorough history, Complete neurological assessment

The nurse should prioritize the trauma primary survey. The primary survey addresses catastrophic hemorrhage, airway protection with cervical spinal immobilization, breathing, and circulation before neurological status to minimize risk for further injury to the spinal cord. After the primary survey is complete, the nurse can gather history for the secondary survey (e.g., medications, allergies, mechanism of injury).

Provide supplemental oxygen

Supplemental oxygen may be required to correct or prevent hypoxia after the cervical spine has been stabilized.

Key Takeaway:

  • It is essential to immobilize the cervical spine as soon as possible for a client with a suspected spinal injury.

  • Following cervical spine stabilization, the nurse should complete a neurological assessment, obtain history, and provide oxygen if indicated.
items.lead: The nurse is caring for a 17-year-old client who was brought to the emergency department by his mother after sustaining head and neck trauma.
items.stem: Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
options: Immobilize the cervical spine.
Provide supplemental oxygen.
Obtain a thorough history of injury.
Complete a neurological assessment.

items.subject: mental-health
items.explanation:
Clients considering suicide may provide verbal and behavioral indicators. Verbal indicators include statements suggesting hopelessness, a desire to escape, or that an ending is near (e.g., “It will all be over soon”). Behavioral indicators include social withdrawal and putting final affairs in order.

If an indicator is present, the nurse must prioritize safety by directly asking if the client is having thoughts of harming themselves [Choice 2].

Clients may be hesitant to discuss feelings of suicide without prompting. By asking directly, the nurse indicates it is safe to talk about these feelings. Open communication allows the treatment team to provide appropriate intervention, care, and support.

Incorrect:

"Is everything okay?”

While this response does address the client's low mood, it does not directly inquire about the client's safety or suicidal thoughts. While showing empathy is important, directly assessing the client’s safety is the highest priority.

Family relationships

This response does not address the client's current suicidal thoughts and immediate safety concerns. While family dynamics and situational stressors are relevant to the client's mental health, it is not the most pressing issue at this moment.

Alcohol use

Substance use may indicate ineffective coping and increases the risk of suicidal behavior. Therefore, the client’s current alcohol use should be assessed. However, it does not take priority over directly asking about suicidal ideation. The client's alcohol consumption can be explored later in the assessment.

Key Takeaway:

  • When indicators of suicidal ideation are present, the priority is to ask about safety directly.
items.lead: The nurse is talking with a client diagnosed with major depressive disorder who has a history of alcohol abuse. The client states, “Nothing matters. It will all be over soon.”
items.stem: Which of the following responses would be the priority?
options: "You seem sad. Is everything okay?”
“Are you having any thoughts of harming yourself?”
"Tell me more about your current relationship with your family."
"You mentioned before you drank alcohol. How often do you drink?”

items.subject: management-of-care
items.explanation:
Continuous cardiac monitoring is needed for clients with potassium imbalances due to the risk of lethal dysrhythmias such as complete heart block, asystole, and ventricular fibrillation.

The nurse should prioritize assessing clients with possible malfunctioning equipment or abnormal monitoring results, such as a client with frequent artifacts on the telemetry monitor [Choice 3].

Artifacts are abnormal rhythm distortions caused by movement or equipment malfunctioning. The nurse should immediately assess the client and the equipment to ensure accurate cardiac rhythm interpretation.

Incorrect:

Atrial fibrillation, metoprolol due

While beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol, atenolol) should be administered on time, a client who has a malfunctioning cardiac monitor should be assessed first. After addressing the cardiac monitor, the nurse should administer medication to this client next.

Bacterial endocarditis, heart rate 105

This heart rate is within normal limits for a 6-year-old client. This client does not have an unexpected or acute event occurring, so they are not the priority for assessment.

Anorexia nervosa, heart rate 50

Clients diagnosed with anorexia nervosa often experience bradycardia secondary to a hypometabolic state. Although this is abnormal, it is expected due to the client’s chronic condition and does not take priority.

Key Takeaway:

  • Clients with hypokalemia require accurate continuous cardiac monitoring due to the risk of life-threatening dysrhythmias.

  • Clients with malfunctioning equipment or abnormal monitor readings require immediate assessment.
items.lead: The nurse has been made aware of the following client situations.
items.stem: The nurse should first assess the client who is
options: 75-years-old with atrial fibrillation and has metoprolol due
6–years-old with bacterial endocarditis and a heart rate of 105
57-years-old with hypokalemia with frequent artifact on the telemetry monitor
17-years-old with anorexia nervosa with a heart rate of 50 and has not eaten today

items.subject: fundamentals
items.explanation:
Droplet precautions prevent transmission of pathogens that are spread via large respiratory droplets produced when a person coughs, sneezes, or talks. These droplets can travel short distances (typically up to 3 ft [1 m]) and come into contact with the mucous membranes of another person.

Droplet precautions require staff and visitors to wear surgical masks when entering the room. Additionally, the client should be placed in a private room or be cohorted with another client with the same infection. The client should also wear a mask during transport outside the room.

Clients with viral respiratory symptoms (e.g., myalgias, chills, rigors, cough) are placed on droplet isolation until infectious status can be confirmed (e.g., through testing for influenza or SARS-CoV-2) [Choice 4].

Group A Streptococcus (GAS), which causes strep throat, is also spread via respiratory droplets and would require droplet precautions [Choice 5].

Incorrect:

Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) with hemoptysis

Clients with TB require airborne precautions, including use of an N95 respirator and a negative pressure room. N95 respirators protect against both airborne and droplet particles.

Herpes simplex virus lesions (HSV) on the mouth and nose

HSV is spread through direct contact with infected lesions or body fluids. HSV requires contact precautions.

Diarrhea with stool culture positive for E. coli O157.H7

E. coli O157.H7 is spread via the fecal-oral route, typically from consuming contaminated food or water or through person-to-person contact. Clients with infectious diarrhea require contact precautions.


Key Takeaway:

Droplet precautions are required for:

  • Viral respiratory infections

  • GAS pharyngitis
items.lead: The nurse is caring for multiple clients in the emergency department.
items.stem: Which of the following client conditions would require the nurse to implement droplet precautions? Select all that apply.
options: Pulmonary tuberculosis with hemoptysis
Herpes simplex virus lesions on the mouth and nose
Diarrhea with stool culture positive for E. coli O157.H7
Myalgias, chills, rigors, and a productive cough for 2 days
Sore throat with culture positive for group A Streptococcus

items.subject: adult-health
items.explanation:
Airway management is a priority for clients with suspected inhalation injuries (e.g., hoarse voice, restlessness, singed nasal hair). Clients with large burns or burns to the face or neck are at high risk for life-threatening airway inflammation due to smoke and heat inhalation. The nurse should first administer high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask [Choice 4].

A non-rebreather mask rapidly delivers high-flow oxygen to improve oxygenation until the client is stabilized. Clients with suspected inhalation injuries are often prophylactically intubated to maintain airway patency even if they do not demonstrate signs of respiratory distress.

Incorrect:

Administer fentanyl

Burns cause severe pain requiring IV opioid analgesics (e.g., morphine, fentanyl). However, airway management is prioritized to prevent respiratory arrest.

Prepare for escharotomy

Extremity circumferential burns can cause compartment syndrome, requiring an escharotomy or fasciotomy. Both are emergent procedures that involve cutting through hardened burned tissue (eschar) or fascia to reduce intracompartmental pressure and restore tissue perfusion. Although an escharotomy helps maintain perfusion, airway management is prioritized.

Administer IV bolus

Large burns increase capillary permeability, causing fluid to leak from capillaries into surrounding tissue. This fluid shift decreases intravascular pressure, causing hypovolemic shock. Warm IV fluids boluses are administered based on the burned surface area using fluid administration calculations (e.g., Parkland formula). Although fluid resuscitation is needed, airway management is prioritized.

Key Takeaway:

  • Clients with burn injuries are at risk for inhalation injuries and hypovolemia.

  • Treatment includes warmed IV fluids, supplemental oxygen, and typically intubation to maintain airway patency.
items.lead: The nurse is caring for a client who sustained burn injuries to the neck, chest, and around the entire left leg. The nurse observes the client is restless, has a hoarse voice, and has decreased pedal pulses in the left foot.
items.stem: Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
options: Provide a dose of fentanyl 25 mcg via IV push.
Prepare the client for an escharotomy of the left leg.
Start an IV bolus of warmed lactated Ringer’s solution.
Administer high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask.

items.subject: adult-health
items.explanation:
Circulating intravascular volume is decreased with prolonged vomiting and poor fluid intake. Low intravascular volume causes decreased renal blood flow and prerenal azotemia (i.e., increased blood urea nitrogen [BUN] and creatinine).

Oliguria, or low urine output (i.e., <30 mL/hr), indicates inadequate renal perfusion and suggests that acute kidney injury (AKI) is developing. Without prompt medical evaluation and treatment, AKI can quickly progress to permanent renal damage [Choice 3].

The nurse should anticipate administering IV fluids to improve renal perfusion along with monitoring kidney function for improvement or worsening (e.g., BUN, creatinine).

Incorrect:

No appetite

Loss of appetite is expected with prolonged vomiting and will usually return once the underlying condition improves. It is not the priority over possible renal damage.

Dizziness

Dehydration and low intravascular volume decrease blood return to the heart. Less circulating volume causes a transient drop in blood pressure when changing position (i.e., orthostatic hypotension). While fall precautions should be implemented, orthostatic hypotension is not a priority over the risk for renal damage.

Temperature 100.2 F (37.9 C)

A low-grade fever is part of a systemic immune response, likely due to an infectious agent causing gastrointestinal symptoms. Antipyretics can be administered; however, a low-grade fever does not pose an immediate threat to the client and is not a priority over the risk for renal damage.

Key Takeaway:

  • Oliguria increases the risk for acute kidney injury development, which can quickly progress to permanent renal damage.
items.lead: The nurse is caring for a client who reports vomiting for the last week.
items.stem: Which of the following findings would be a priority for the nurse to report to the primary health care provider?
options: Client has no appetite.
Dizziness upon standing
Urine output of 20 mL/hr
Temperature of 100.2 F (37.9 C)

items.subject: fundamentals
items.explanation:
Airborne precautions are used with pathogens, like tuberculosis (TB), that spread through small airborne droplets and remain suspended in the air for extended periods (e.g., talking, coughing, sneezing).

When transport outside the client’s room is required, the client should wear a surgical mask to prevent pathogen spread [Choice 4].

Incorrect:

Share room

Two clients requiring airborne precautions, even when infected with the same illness, should not share rooms due to the increased risk of cross-infection or reinfection.

Positive pressure room

A private, filtered, positive-pressure airflow room prevents potentially contaminated outside air from entering the room. It is used specifically for immunocompromised clients. A negative air pressure room is used for TB, which uses a High-Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) filter, preventing contaminated air from escaping the client’s room.

Surgical mask within 6 feet

Surgical masks are used for droplet precautions and do not filter all smaller airborne particles. The nurse should wear an N95 mask at all times while in the client’s room, as these are more protective.

Key Takeaway:

Clients with airborne illness require:

  • A private room

  • Airborne precautions (e.g., N95 masks)

  • A surgical mask during transport
items.lead: The nurse is planning a staff education program about tuberculosis (TB).
items.stem: Which of the following information should the nurse include?
options: Two clients with TB can share the same room.
Clients should be placed in a positive pressure room.
A surgical mask must be worn within 6 feet of the client.
Clients need to wear a surgical mask when being transported.

items.subject: adult-health
items.explanation:
Colorectal cancer (CRC) originates in the colon or rectum. Several risk factors can increase risk for colorectal cancer:

  • Older age

  • Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (i.e., Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis)

  • Personal or family history of colorectal polyps or colorectal cancer

  • Genetic mutations (e.g., Lynch syndrome)

  • Diet low in fiber, fruits, and vegetables, or high in red or processed meats [Choice 3]. Processed meats (bacon, sausages, hot dogs) have carcinogenic preservatives and chemicals.

  • Being sedentary or obese

  • Alcohol and tobacco use

Incorrect:

Dysphagia after stroke
Clients with dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) are at risk for aspiration, which can cause pneumonia. While this is a significant concern, it does not increase the risk for colorectal cancer.

Ibuprofen daily
Prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) increases risk for peptic ulcer disease (PUD), which affects the lining of the stomach and small intestine. However, PUD does not increase risk for colorectal cancer.

Lost weight after gastric bypass
Clients who undergo gastric bypass are at risk for vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia) because they no longer have gastric tissue- producing intrinsic factor. Rapid weight loss can also lead to the formation of gallstones and cholecystitis. However, these factors do not increase risk for colorectal cancer.

Key Takeaway:

Factors increasing risk for colorectal cancer include:

  • Older age, IBD, or having a personal or family history of polyps or colorectal cancer (nonmodifiable)

  • Alcohol or tobacco use, obesity and sedentary lifestyle, or diet high in red or processed meat (modifiable)
items.lead: The nurse is screening clients for those at risk for colorectal cancer.
items.stem: At highest risk for colorectal cancer is the client who
options: has dysphagia after experiencing a stroke
takes ibuprofen daily for chronic joint pain
consumes a diet high in red and processed meats
lost 200 lbs (90.7 kg) after a gastric bypass surgery

items.subject: child-health
items.explanation:
Tachypnea, hypoxemia, adventitious breath sounds (e.g., wheezing), and use of accessory muscles (i.e., retractions) all indicate respiratory insufficiency and require immediate intervention [Choices 1, 4, 5, and 6]. Alterations in level of consciousness (e.g., lethargy) occur when the brain receives insufficient oxygen, which further suggests respiratory insufficiency.

Without immediate intervention, this client may progress to respiratory failure, leading to decreased oxygen delivery to the tissues (hypoxia), eventually causing organ damage.

Incorrect:

Temperature

The temperature is slightly elevated but not concerning. However, it is not prioritized over respiratory symptoms that affect airway and breathing.

Clubbed fingers

In clients with CF, chronic hypoxia stimulates peripheral vasodilation, especially in the hands. Over time, this causes clubbing or rounding of the fingernail beds. Since this is an expected chronic symptom, it is not immediately concerning.

Integumentary assessment
An elevated body temperature can cause diaphoresis. Small abrasions and injuries are common incidental findings in children and are less concerning than respiratory insufficiency.

Frequent, foul-smelling, bulky stool

In clients with CF, mucus blocks the release of enzymes into the intestines, causing malabsorption of fat. Steatorrhea occurs when malabsorption of fat in the intestines leads to excess fat in the stool. This causes stool to become oily, bulky, and foul-smelling. Although this is an abnormal finding, it does not take precedence over respiratory insufficiency.

Key Takeaway:

  • Signs of respiratory insufficiency include low oxygen saturation, increased respiratory rate, wheezing, retractions, and lethargy.

  • Respiratory insufficiency is the immediate concern.

items.subject: child-health
items.explanation:
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder characterized by mutations of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene. In normal physiology, CFTR protein channels pump chloride and water into bodily secretions, keeping them thin and slippery. Altered CFTR channels inhibit chloride and water movement, producing thick, sticky mucus in multiple organ systems (e.g., gastrointestinal, reproductive, respiratory).

Excess mucus lines the bronchioles of the lungs and narrows the lower airways to create a whistling sound or wheezing.

Therefore, the nurse should recognize that wheezing in this client is likely caused by excess mucus due to cystic fibrosis.

Incorrect:

Bronchospasm, Asthma exacerbation
Bronchospasm is constriction of the bronchioles or airways. This constriction is frequently caused by an asthma exacerbation due to an excessive inflammatory response in response to a trigger. Given her productive cough and thick drainage, excess mucus is the more likely cause.

Upper airway inflammation, Epiglottitis

Upper airway inflammation can be caused by infection or irritation of the upper airway. Epiglottitis is typically caused by H. influenzae infection. This infection causes rapid swelling of the epiglottis that results in a sore throat, drooling, and a “froggy” voice. Upper airway inflammation from epiglottitis or other conditions can cause high-pitched respirations or stridor, not wheezing.

Key Takeaway:

  • The primary symptom of cystic fibrosis is excess, thick mucus production in various organ systems.

  • Mucus blocks and narrows the airways, causing wheezing.

items.subject: child-health
items.explanation:
Cystic fibrosis (CF) causes mucous membranes to produce thick, sticky mucus. The mucus is so thick it cannot be expelled with coughing and accumulates along bronchiole walls.

Copious, thick mucus traps bacteria within the lungs, causing chronic infections like pneumonia [Choice 2]. The buildup of thick airway secretions also causes bronchodilation to compensate and improve airflow. Chronic airway dilation eventually becomes irreversible, known as bronchiectasis [Choice 5].

Thick mucus also blocks the release of pancreatic enzymes, causing malabsorption of intestinal nutrients, as indicated by this client’s bulky, foul-smelling stool [Choice 3].

Incorrect:

Sepsis

Sepsis is an overwhelming immune and inflammatory response to infection. This child has signs that could indicate an infection; however, the clinical picture is more consistent with a cystic fibrosis exacerbation that will not progress to sepsis if managed appropriately.

Pleural effusion

Pleural effusion is fluid accumulation within the pleural space. The most common cause in children is pneumonia. This client may develop pleural effusion secondary to pneumonia but is not currently at risk.

Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is air accumulation within the pleural space often caused by tissue trauma from physical injury or illness. In CF, chronic lung damage can cause recurrent pneumothoraces. However, this usually occurs in older clients with advanced CF and is not immediately concerning.

Key Takeaway:

  • CF causes trapping of bacteria in the lungs, resulting in frequent or chronic pneumonia.

  • Long-term buildup of secretions in the airways causes permanent bronchiole dilation.

  • Mucus blocks the release of pancreatic enzymes, resulting in malabsorption.

items.subject: child-health
items.explanation:
In cystic fibrosis (CF), interventions focus on providing respiratory and nutritional support.

Indicated interventions include:

  • Chest x-ray and nasopharyngeal culture to diagnose potential respiratory infection [Choices 1 and 3].

  • Chest physiotherapy (CPT), which utilizes percussion, vibration, and postural drainage to mobilize and clear respiratory secretions [Choice 4].

  • Hypertonic saline (i.e., mucolytic) via nebulizer, which draws fluid into the airways, thinning secretions. This medication also replaces sodium absent in secretions due to CFTR mutation [Choice 6].

  • Positive expiratory pressure therapy (PEP) [Choice 8]. In PEP therapy, the client blows through a resistance valve, which increases positive airway pressure to open airways.

  • Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) to facilitate nutrient absorption [Choice 9]. Thickened mucus clogs pancreatic ducts, which prevents enzyme release into the intestines, inhibiting nutrient absorption.

Not indicated:

  • A thoracentesis removes fluid from the pleural space (i.e., pleural effusion), which this client is not experiencing [Choice 2].

  • Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) is administered to clients who are unable to digest or consume adequate oral nutrition. Although the client is experiencing malabsorption, oral intake with PERT is preferred due to risks associated with TPN (e.g., sepsis) [Choice 5].

  • Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) provides constant pressure to keep the airways open [Choice 7]. The client’s oxygen saturation is 94% on low-dose oxygen; therefore, she does not currently require additional oxygen support.

Key Takeaway:

Interventions for CF include:

  • Diagnostic testing for infection

  • Mucolytics (hypertonic saline) to thin secretions

  • CPT to mobilize secretions

  • PERT to support nutrient absorption

items.subject: child-health
items.explanation:
In healthy digestion, digestive enzymes are secreted from the pancreas into the intestines. In cystic fibrosis (CF), the pancreatic duct becomes plugged with thickened mucus, damaging pancreatic tissue and obstructing enzyme transport. Therefore, the pancreas cannot secrete effective amounts of amylase, lipase, and protease enzymes, which are responsible for the breakdown and absorption of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins, respectively. Malabsorption of these nutrients will eventually cause malnutrition.

Appropriate interventions at mealtime include:

  • Providing a high-protein and high-calorie diet to improve the likelihood of protein absorption and meet increased energy requirements caused by increased work of breathing.

  • Administering pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT), which provides synthetic versions of missing enzymes. PERT is administered with food to improve nutrient absorption.

Incorrect:

Provide low-fat diet

Clients with CF are unable to properly absorb fat and nutrients in the intestines; therefore, fat and caloric intake should be unrestricted. Further, clients often require high-calorie, high-protein foods, and supplemental fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) with enough dietary fat for optimal vitamin absorption.

Administer metformin

Clients with CF can develop type 1 diabetes related to damaged pancreatic tissue. Metformin (biguanide) treats type 2 diabetes by increasing insulin sensitivity and inhibiting gluconeogenesis, which will not benefit clients with CF.

Provide low-sodium diet
Clients with CF waste sodium and chloride through sweat due to the inappropriate movement of these electrolytes across epithelial cells. The client requires a high-sodium diet.

Key Takeaway:

Management of gastrointestinal symptoms includes:

  • A high-protein, high-sodium diet

  • Unrestricted fat intake

  • PERT administered with food
