items.explanation:
Discharge education for clients with cystic fibrosis (CF) includes managing respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms, preventing complications, and counseling regarding the genetic and chronic nature of CF.

Teaching was effective if the mother understands the following points:

  • CF increases diabetes risk due to long-term pancreatic insufficiency [Choice 1]. Clients with both diabetes and CF have complex nutritional needs that focus on maximizing nutrient absorption while managing blood glucose levels.

  • Mutated CF transmembrane conductance regulator channels cause increased sodium excretion through sweat. Parents often notice a “salty taste” when kissing their children [Choice 3].

  • Thicker cervical mucus in the female reproductive tract can block sperm from fertilizing eggs, potentially causing infertility in women [Choice 5].

  • CF is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder inherited when both parents carry a recessive copy of the gene. If two individuals with the recessive gene have children, there is a 1 in 4 (25%) chance that any given child will inherit two copies of the gene and develop CF [Choice 6].

Corrected teaching:

  • CF increases the risk for secondary infections. Timely vaccination is critical to preventing illness [Choice 2]. This client does not have conditions that require a modified vaccine schedule (e.g., heart disease, immunocompromised).

  • CF is a chronic disease with no cure [Choice 4]. Treatment focuses on improving quality of life and increasing lifespan.

Key Takeaway:

  • “Salty-tasting” skin is an early sign of CF.

  • CF increases diabetes risk due to long-term pancreatic insufficiency.

  • CF is an autosomal recessive inherited disorder with no cure.

items.subject: management-of-care
items.explanation:
Advocacy is acting on behalf of the client to ensure the client’s rights are respected. This includes respecting the client’s autonomy—the right to make independent care decisions.

A client who is competent to make decisions has the right to refuse treatment, including a feeding tube. The nurse should notify the health care provider of the client’s decision so the care team does not proceed without the client’s consent [Choice 4].

Incorrect:

Choice 1: Not daughter’s decision
Although the statement may be accurate, it is confrontational and does not best demonstrate advocacy. The nurse should use therapeutic communication with the daughter while supporting the client’s autonomy by communicating the client’s stated preference to the health care provider.

Choice 2: Schedule procedure
Scheduling the procedure based on the family’s request would override the client’s stated wishes and violate the client’s autonomy. The nurse should protect the client’s right to make decisions about personal care.

Choice 3: Document and wait

Documentation is important, but the nurse should not delay action until the family agrees. Advocacy means supporting the client’s right to refuse treatment by communicating the client’s wishes to the health care provider.

Key Takeaway:

  • Advocacy means protecting the client's autonomy or right to make decisions by communicating the client's wishes to the care team.

items.subject: child-health
items.explanation:
Epiglottitis is a croup syndrome, often caused by H. influenzae, that results in severe inflammation of the epiglottis (i.e., upper larynx). While croup is characterized by a seal-bark cough, epiglottitis is distinguished by the absence of cough. Other findings of epiglottitis include fever, drooling, agitation, muffled voice, and a swollen, red throat.

If untreated, upper airway swelling in epiglottitis can quickly progress to airway obstruction and respiratory failure. Therefore, the nurse should assess the client’s respiratory status, contact the health care provider immediately, and prepare for possible endotracheal intubation [Choice 3]. Stimulating the gag reflex can cause the throat to close and obstruct the airway. Therefore, the nurse should avoid inspecting the throat except immediately before an emergency intubation or tracheostomy.

Incorrect:

Administer dextromethorphan

Cough suppressants (e.g., dextromethorphan) may dry and thicken respiratory secretions and should be avoided in children <4 years old due to potentially serious side effects. Instead, treatment should include antipyretics, IV fluids, and antibiotics (e.g., cefotaxime, vancomycin).

Take oral temperature; Collect respiratory throat culture

Placing objects (e.g., oral temperature probe, throat culture swab) in the client’s mouth can stimulate the gag reflex, leading to spasm of the epiglottis and complete airway obstruction. The nurse should use another route for taking the client’s temperature (e.g., axillary).

Key Takeaway:

  • Epiglottitis is severe inflammation of the epiglottis that can quickly progress to respiratory failure if prompt intervention is not taken.

  • Avoid stimulating the gag reflex or administering cough medication in clients with epiglottitis.

items.subject: adult-health
items.explanation:
After a stroke, a client with hemiparesis (one-sided weakness) should dress the affected side first. Guiding the weaker extremity through the clothing first makes dressing easier and reduces pulling on the affected limb, preventing injury and joint displacement.

This client has right-sided weakness and should place the right arm into the shirt sleeve first. Therefore, the nurse should follow up when the client states that the left arm will be placed into the sleeve first [Choice 2].

No follow-up:

Choice 1: Cane in left hand
The cane should be held on the stronger side, which is the client’s left side. The cane moves forward with the weaker right leg to provide balance and support.

Choice 3: Support right side
When assisting the client to stand, the caregiver should support the client’s weaker right side to prevent a loss of balance. Additionally, the caregiver should stand slightly behind the client if assisting with ambulation.

Choice 4: Left leg first
When stepping up onto a curb, the client should lead with the stronger leg. Because this client has right-sided weakness, the left leg should step up first, followed by the weaker right leg and cane.

Key Takeaway

Clients with one-sided weakness should:

  • Dress the weaker side first.

  • Hold the cane on the strong side.

  • Lead with the strong leg going upstairs.

  • Lead with the weaker leg going downstairs.

  • Have caregivers support the client’s weaker side.

items.subject: fundamentals
items.explanation:
When responding to an equipment malfunction, the nurse should ensure the client’s safety and remove faulty equipment from service to prevent further harm.

The nurse must notify the provider of the medication error so the client can be assessed for complications such as fluid overload and the plan of care can be adjusted if needed. The nurse must remove all malfunctioning equipment from service for inspection [Choice 1]. The malfunctioning pump should be clearly labeled as “do not use,” stored separately from functioning equipment, and sent for biomedical or maintenance evaluation according to facility policy.

Incorrect:

Choice 2: Decrease the IV infusion rate
The nurse should not independently change the prescribed infusion rate to compensate for the extra fluid administered. If the client’s fluid rate needs adjustment, the provider should be notified and the prescribed rate revised as indicated.

Choice 3: Reset pump and continue
A pump that has malfunctioned should not be used because the malfunction could recur. If IV therapy must continue, use a functioning replacement pump instead.

Choice 4: Incident report in medical record
An incident report should be completed for the equipment-related error, but it is not part of the client’s medical record and should not be referenced in the chart. The nurse should document the client assessment, volume of fluid received, and interventions in the health record.

Key Takeaway:

For equipment-related errors:

  • Assess client and notify provider.

  • Remove and place a tag on malfunctioning equipment.

  • Send equipment for evaluation and complete incident reporting.

Registered nurses (RNs) should only delegate tasks that satisfy the five rights of delegation and are within the delegatee’s scope of practice. The RN cannot delegate TAPE tasks (teaching, assessment, planning, and evaluation) because they require the RN’s clinical judgment.

Applying a prescribed silver sulfadiazine cream is medication administration and requires the nurse to assess the pressure injury, verify the prescription, and evaluate the client’s response [Choice 3]. Therefore, the charge nurse should intervene if the RN delegates this task to the UAP.

Appropriate delegation:

Choices 1 & 2: Reposition quadriplegic; Apply antiembolism stockings
Repositioning and applying antiembolism stockings are routine, noninvasive tasks that help prevent complications such as pressure injuries and blood clots. These tasks may be delegated to the UAP with clear instructions from the RN.

Choice 4: Apply dressing over a healed surgical incision
Covering a healed incision with a clean, dry dressing is a routine, nonsterile task that does not require medication administration or assessment. The UAP should report any unexpected redness, drainage, or opening of the incision to the RN.

Key Takeaway:

  • UAPs may provide routine skin care, reposition clients, and change linens.

  • Medication administration, including applying a prescribed medicated ointment, cannot be delegated to the UAP.
